Experienced in TEKNOFEST, I build end-to-end solutions using YOLO, TensorRT on NVIDIA Jetson, and STM32 hardware integration. I love turning complex ideas into working prototypes under pressure. Looking for motivated teammates in frontend/UI, data science, or backend/CAD to build an impactful project together for this NASA challenge!
summary: AstroVital is an offline-first web app that helps astronauts monitor, understand and act on their own health during long-duration missions, when help from Earth may be minutes away. Crew members log vital signs, sleep, mood, radiation dose and exercise. A deterministic, source-cited rules engine evaluates each value against thresholds adapted to the mission environment (ISS, deep-space spacecraft, lunar rover, Moon or Mars base) and shows the result on an interactive body map, using color, icon and text together. Every alert explains what happened, why it matters, what to do now and when to involve the Crew Medical Officer or the flight surgeon; on Mars it switches to autonomous guidance because of the communication delay. A daily, weekly and monthly measurement routine based on NASA, CSA and ESA practice aboard the ISS, adherence-based gamification and an astronaut companion keep health monitoring part of daily life. A separate offline Python tool demonstrates personal-baseline anomaly detection on public wearable data. AstroVital is a prototype decision-support tool that uses simulated crew data; it is not a medical device.
details:
What it does

AstroVital turns a handful of daily measurements into a clear answer to three questions an astronaut asks when no doctor is next to them: Am I okay? What should I do now? When do I call for help?

  • Collect: blood pressure, heart rate, SpO₂, respiration rate, body temperature, blood glucose, sleep, mood, radiation dose and exercise, entered by keyboard on the Measure screen, with large, glove-friendly touch targets throughout the interface.
  • Assess: a deterministic rules engine (no AI at runtime) checks each value against threshold bands adapted to the mission environment, cumulative radiation against the NASA-STD-3001 career limit, solar particle event spikes, trends over time and sustained changes over several days.
  • Explain and guide: every alert follows the same structure: what happened, why it matters in space, what to do now, and when to escalate (self-care, Crew Medical Officer, flight surgeon, emergency). Red results always ask the astronaut to re-measure first.
  • Show: an interactive body map: tap a region to see what it does, how NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight affect it, and its current status; crew overview and live vitals.
  • Routine: a mission-time schedule of daily, weekly and monthly checks based on ISS practice (morning vitals, daily dosimeter reading, exercise six days a week, weekly health summary, monthly examination). Each task is upcoming, due, done, done late or missed.
  • Motivation: XP, levels, streaks, badges, a team score and an astronaut companion. XP rewards adherence only, never "good" values, so there is no incentive to falsify entries.

How it addresses the space hazards

The app models five mission environments (ISS, deep-space spacecraft, lunar rover, lunar base, Mars base). Each one changes expected radiation dose, threshold shifts (for example the higher core body temperature observed in microgravity) and communication delay. On Mars, where a one-way signal can take many minutes, escalation switches from "call the flight surgeon" to an autonomous protocol with an asynchronous report to the ground.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Gives non-medical crew members plain-language, stress-readable guidance instead of raw numbers.
  • Makes regular self-monitoring a habit, so slow changes are caught before they become critical.
  • Works fully offline: no backend, no network calls; it can run from a static folder on a spacecraft network, and each user's data stays in their own browser.
  • The same approach can help people in remote or isolated settings on Earth (Antarctic stations, ships, rural care).

How we built it

React 19, TypeScript and Vite; Zustand for persisted local state; Zod for validated data import/export; Framer Motion for animation; Base UI and Lucide for accessible components and icons; i18next for an English/Turkish interface; Vitest for tests; GitHub Actions for CI and GitHub Pages hosting. A separate offline Python tool builds a multi-day synthetic crew dataset from the public MMASH wearable dataset (PhysioNet) and runs an explainable personal-baseline anomaly detector. Four engineers worked on separate modules (intake, assessment, visualization, core and routine) behind shared, documented contracts, with every change reviewed in a pull request.

What makes it creative

  • Space is not Earth: thresholds shift by environment, and the measurement schedule follows real ISS routines instead of a generic health app.
  • Gamification that rewards doing the check, not the result.
  • Escalation that adapts to communication delay.

Factors we considered

Medical accuracy (every threshold and recommendation is linked to a cited source in docs/SOURCES.md), accessibility (large touch targets, high contrast, color always paired with icon and text), stress-time readability, privacy (simulated data only, no real health data), offline operation and honest limits.

Limitations

AstroVital is a prototype decision-support and training tool, not a medical device. All crew data is simulated. Thresholds are configurable starting points from cited sources, not medical advice. Camera-based heart rate and ultrasound input are planned but not complete in this version.
